title: Savile Row — the address Verne got wrong
learning_goal: Know that Verne put Fogg at No. 7 and Sheridan's death there in 1814, that Sheridan lived at No. 14 and died in 1816, and that the Row was already tailoring country; feel the hush of cloth and chalk.

narration.script: Here we are: the corner of Burlington Gardens and Savile Row. Verne opens the novel on this spot — 'No. 7, Saville Row, Burlington Gardens, the house in which Sheridan died in 1814.' He spells the street with two Ls, and he is wrong twice more. Sheridan the playwright lived at No. 14, not No. 7, and he died there in 1816, not 1814. Watch the doors as we walk and look for the numbers: No. 14 carries the plaque, put up in 1881. There is no plaque for Fogg anywhere. So the novel is our guidebook, not our gospel; we will correct it with a smile whenever we can. Look in the windows now — bolts of cloth, chalk marks, half-made jackets. This was already tailoring country in 1872. Henry Poole put his front door on the Row in 1846 and is still here — since 1982 at No. 15. Poole's own story is that in 1865 they cut the Prince of Wales a short evening jacket — the ancestor, they say, of the dinner jacket. One small detour in time: on the roof of No. 3, on the thirtieth of January 1969, the Beatles played their rooftop concert. Fogg's house, in the book, ran on the newest kit of its day — gas for light and warmth, electric bells, speaking-tubes — and held not a single book, because his club had two libraries. Here is the Row around 1890, a few years after Fogg. Same doors. Same hush.
